title: How browser-based file compression works
description: From the moment you drop a file to the moment you download the result, every step runs on your own device. Here is the real pipeline, without the marketing.

featuredImage.alt: Folders pass through a green press inside a browser-shaped frame.

seoDescription: A walkthrough of the real client-side compression pipeline: magic-byte validation, worker and WebAssembly engines, and why no step needs a server.

body.text: FileCompresser reads and processes selected files in your browser tab. The page downloads its interface and processing code, while the file itself stays on your device during processing.
Step one: the file is checked before anything is processed

The first thing that happens is not compression. Before an encoder is even loaded, the file is inspected: its size is checked against the limit for that tool, and its first bytes are compared against known file signatures — the PNG magic number, the JPEG SOI marker, the ZIP local file header.

This matters more than it sounds. A file called photo.jpg could be anything. Renaming a program to .jpg is trivial, and a tool that trusts the extension will happily hand it to a decoder. Checking the actual bytes is what makes "this looks like a PDF, which this tool does not support" a real answer rather than a guess.
Step two: an engine is loaded, and only the one you need

Image compression uses a Web Worker where supported, with browser canvas operations also used for decoding and target-size encoding. Heavy work can still affect responsiveness on constrained devices. Video, audio and GIF work uses a WebAssembly build of FFmpeg — about 21 MB of code, downloaded once and cached, and never loaded on a page you are not using it on.

None of that engine code is fetched until you actually start a job. A page view costs you the site's own JavaScript and nothing else. The distinction matters for the same reason the compression does: the work happens on your machine, and the code that does it is only ever code.

body.caption: The full path of a file, from selection to download.

body.text: Step three: the output is a real file, or an honest failure

When the encoder finishes, you get a Blob — an actual file in memory, with a real byte count and a real MIME type. If the result came out larger than the input, the tool says so in words rather than presenting a bigger file as a success.

Some outputs are validated before you are offered them. A compressed PDF is parsed again and its page count compared against the original; if the round trip does not hold, you get an error instead of a broken download. ZIP entries are checked for path traversal before a single byte is written to disk.

body.title: The whole point
body.text: No step in that pipeline needs a server. That is not a feature toggle — it is the reason the tools are built this way.
